p:
Uh, thank you for the question, Chair. I can start just at the top level, and then I, I do want to address the- some of the outreach. I think I think in regards to forward-facing materials. So, um, really, you know, and what SBS pay is, is always a goal for an agency to ensure that immigration is not an afterthought, but it's truly embedded in the work. And I think what our colleague here expresses is really showcases that, um, the work that we do with them is really threefold. We support them with, uh, language access and provide technical assistance as they're developing, um, material and, you know, interpreting the law and the Local Law 30. We also partner with them in outreach events. Um, we have partnered with them just this calendar year in 4, 4 events, but it doesn't stop there. We also

provide them with policy updates that might relate to their work. In addition to what was mentioned, some of the outreach material that we've put together and sort of to the comment that you made, um, we made changes to our forward-facing material to ensure that there was a Know Your Rights, a flyer that was provided in regards to what individuals could do if ICE comes into their workplace. CHAIRPERSON ENCARNACIÓN: Yeah, and is, uh, SBS on the interagency task force?

Yes, they are. CHAIRPERSON ENCARNACIÓN: Okay, um, and so, you know, just yesterday we were in a meeting and one of our colleagues, Council Member Zhuang, mentioned many of her businesses, uh, small businesses, they're not on the web, on the internet in terms of a website. They just don't have that kind of access or that kind of support. And so obviously this is a community that, you know, it's operating in a different language. Many immigrant communities, many immigrant business owners, were trying to get connected into what was going on with the FIFA World Cup, um, and really wanted to understand how, um, how we can

support. Because I think the point I was trying to make with the amount of staff and the amount of resources is that there's always gonna be room for people to fall through the cracks, right? But in a time when we're talking about serious consequences, about deportation, about fear of being able to stay in this country, like we have to tighten up those resources to make sure that they don't. So I just wanted to understand, like, in, in those cases, where would any one of my colleagues reach out to here to really, uh, close that loop?

So I know, Chair, you're, you're, I think you kind of referenced FIFA, right? Is that kind of part of the— CHAIRPERSON ENCARNACIÓN: Yeah. I mean, I think it's an example of a larger issue. I mean, this is a huge thing coming into New York, and we still have small businesses that are unable to gain access to that.

So I think for us, you know, I did— we do have a 6-person, 5 to 6, currently at 5-person outreach team. Um, the— we also operate 7 business solution centers, one in each borough. We also have a hotline, 888-SBS-4NYC. And particularly to your

point on website accessibility and the digital literacy gap, that website, the digital divide, that, that website is supposed to serve as a more friendly, warm handoff space to get connected to services instead of logging onto the website and then, uh, going through 10 different tabs to figure out what you need. But you've got the hotline, you've got 7 business solution centers. We have, um, our in-person team that is also going out to neighborhoods. Certainly more would help, but we have been committed to maximizing every resource that we have to deliver what we can. And, uh, proud that we just started our FIFA outreach work as soon as, uh, the materials were finalized by our partner agencies. And within a week, you know, we're sharing 56,000 New Yorkers have been able to reach and, um, have reached, ah, have received these materials. Certainly we're gonna spend the next month doubling down on this 'cause we know that this is not enough in a lot of neighborhoods. Um- CHAIRPERSON ENCARNACIÓN: Okay.

We're not receiving enough materials. So we got, we're gonna go out there. We

would love your support as well in this critical time where we only have, right, 60, less than 60 days. So we're gonna do our best with the resources we have. We know our partner agencies are gonna do their best. Um, and any support we can get from community partners, local electeds, we would absolutely love that. And then at our Small Business Month Expo, which is our flagship largest ever small business gathering for the year, which we'd love again, everybody too, uh, please do share it in your newsletters and engage with your constituents. We're gonna have not only tabling by tourism and other partners that will promote again some of these opportunities, to the 2,500+ people that show up in person. We're also gonna have a panel discussion, uh, during that day with Mia, who's our czar for World Cup, with the president of the tourism— NYC Tourism, with, uh, leadership from SBS to further share from the top on all of the ways in which we want people to engage there. We're getting to a point where there's almost, I think it's 8 different ways in which small businesses can engage and benefit from existing efforts that could help them with marketing, that

could help them with some visibility. That's a lot of things to keep track of and so we're, we're intentionally trying to make sure it's in a toolkit that people can access with QR code and links, hyperlinks. It's also in person when we're talking to people, we're pointing them to the QR code. It's also at our large-scale events in the expo, and it's also being shared through our, uh, email marketing. And of the 56,000 folks that we reached, that includes every single food service establishment that has an email with the Department of Health. We get that list, and we've made sure every single restaurant business, food business that we have a contact for, has received that information. CHAIRPERSON ENCARNACIÓN: Okay. And, um, for MOIA, what have you learned about the, um, those working in the fields like hospitality and construction about the efforts, uh, the effects of— excuse me— of immigration policies on the workforce and their business operations?

Uh, thank you for the question, Chair. Um, if you would allow me to take a bit of a step back, um, because just some data for you is that

via our, um, Ask MOIA hotline and and, um, service that we do within MOIA. Um, we've only received 10 calls connected to just, uh, a small business specifically, but it's really been more about, um, how to access, um, legal services more than like directly on small businesses. But just to sort of say that, um, at MOIA we support immigrants as a whole. Uh, immigrant entrepreneurs are just one piece of the puzzle in the larger spectrum. We provide support to immigrant New Yorkers and just to provide you with a bit of a stack to really sort of answer your question. Undocumented immigrants have the highest labor participation, as you noted, of any group, yet they earn the lowest. Undocumented immigrants earn an average of about $36,000 compared to naturalized noncitizens who make about $50,000. The biggest concern we've heard just as a whole in regards to immigrants, um, is, uh, remaining in status. Um, right now, as we've seen and as, as has been noted, um, the federal Administration and any hopes of affirmative relief has really been halted. And the fear of even submitting an application for citizenship, um, people

just don't want to because they're afraid of what might happen if they show up to a ceremony. So, um, the bulk of the work that we've provided and the bulk of resources have been for our legal services that make up about 90% of the funding that we give out. CHAIRPERSON ENCARNACIÓN: I, I agree. I've heard a lot, a lot of, um, that feedback as well. And I know that, um, while we're talking about what can be done, I think the frustration that all of us feel is that there's very— we're very limited as a city, and we're trying to understand how we can best support both of your offices to make sure that that, you know, individuals are being supported, whether that be by language access, making sure that, you know, um, flyers and QR codes. I think those are great, but some of them just don't operate in that way. So I'm glad that we're going out into the streets. I also, I'm gonna encourage obviously that the expo be, you know, bring it uptown, bring it to the Bronx, bring it, bring it in other places. We'll find a space for you, you know, just, I know, we, we, we wanna make sure that it's accessible and that everybody feels a part of it. And it's not somewhere

Midtown where people may not, you know, may not be familiar with and may not care to go to. So it's just, you know, that accessibility and that real compassion and care of saying like, we'll come to you, I think really works well with small businesses, especially because they have a lot on their plate as it is. So, uh, put that out there before I, I open it up to the other Council Members, uh, so that they can have some questions but thank you.

As you've put it out there, um, we'll say if there's an opportunity, if you identify a location, a venue, an event that's already happening or something you'd want to work with us on, we'd be happy to bring our resources too. And we've, we've done a series of events, uh, in the district with the— your office and your predecessor, uh, when you were running that office as Chief of Staff. And, uh, and we're committed to that work. We want to be in every neighborhood. We're going to be in Little Senegal again for FIFA, and we've been in East Harlem even last week doing some outreach to local bodegas and delis, uh, as the city-owned grocery store conversation picks up. And so we're committed to

this work. We'll be anywhere and everywhere you invite us to reach out to our teams and we'll figure out the best way to staff. CHAIRPERSON ENCARNACIÓN: I love that and let's go both ways. If you're in my neighborhood, I should know and go.
Yes, yes. CHAIRPERSON ENCARNACIÓN: Alright, thank you.
Thank you. I will now turn it over to Council Member Morano for questions.

Thank you both, Madam Chairs, for convening this hearing and for your leadership of each of these, uh, Committees. Thank you for your testimony. Um, just following up on what everyone else was mentioning on the World Cup, I know that you said that SBS is coordinating for the World Cup, and you expect incredible foot traffic. What specific steps are being taken to ensure outer borough businesses, small businesses, including Staten Island businesses, actually benefit economically instead of all the activity being concentrated in Manhattan tourist zones?

Thank you, uh, Council Member. I think that really it's the leadership of our Mayor and our— the first ever World Cup czar who ensured that the 5 uh, fan events, the 5, 5 fine zones that the city was gonna work with the host committee on, uh, organizing, uh, are being organized in all boroughs and that they're free, which is different than what was intended initially. Um, that itself I think signals this direction of ensuring outer boroughs are represented and can, uh, engage with the economic opportunity. Then there's this series of opportunities that are being planned. You could engage in any business in New York City, including outer borough businesses could engage in this, uh, 5-borough um, we'll get the exact name— Five Borough Tournament, I think it's called— where you could sign up for the $26 special and you'll be promoted as part of tourism's marketing material. So when tourists go in, they wanna explore the list of people who are participating in this Five Borough Tournament, you could see yourself listed there. Uh, there's a calendar of events that, uh, tourism is also putting together where businesses can be featured if they're doing FIFA-related engagement.

Um, and so there's— and there's a toolkit that we've developed with— that tourism has developed in coordination with us that lists all of these different types of engagements. Again, it's almost 8 different ways in which a business can participate in some of these free marketing opportunities for themselves. And so it's a lot, it's a bit overwhelming now. That's how many, uh, ways there are to engage. And so we are taking that to Port Richmond, we're taking that to Little Haiti. Uh, we'll— we've shared it across, um, the business contacts that we have, and we're gonna commit over the next month to doing that outreach, um, to ensure that businesses can benefit from these opportunities.

In your testimony, you repeatedly mentioned outreach, resource fairs, translated materials, and know your rights information, which is— which is great. But w— what measurable economic outcomes can you point to? H— have business closures decreased? Has foot traffic improved? Have revenues stabilized? And I don't mean to sound cynical when I ask the question, but are we mostly measuring success by the measure— by

the number of flyers distributed and events held. Do those translate into real-world economic impact?

So there's, there's opportunities for businesses to really, uh, plug into this World Cup, right? And there's, and there's things that they could do even today without any of these opportunities that we've been mentioning today in this hearing. Um, a business, if it's part of their natural course to have games that are streamed, all that can continue. vThey don't need licenses from FIFA, they don't need a permit from SEPO, they don't need any other additional step. If they are a nightlife business in the North Shore and they already play, uh, a game— games on their TVs, all of that can continue. They could easily just market it as like, this is a FIFA game night and you can come in, um, and there's some basic rules but incredibly easy to follow. In most cases, they don't need to have any additional changes to their practices. And so we know naturally there's gonna be an economic gain from just doing what they do. Uh, we as a city and at SBS, what we're committed to is where the city is intentionally creating opportunities for free

marketing, let's spread those out across the city so they could benefit. The city's also working, uh, in City Hall, uh, under their leadership, um, working towards a culture, a cultural passport. That would also feature different neighborhoods where you can engage with the countries that are being featured in the World Cup. That again, whenever that information comes out, we'll be promoting it. So as things come out from our partner agencies, we're spreading the word. Um, and, and to your point, there's natural economic growth that will happen because people are gonna— business owners are gonna be creative, and it's New York City, they're always creative. Um, but to the extent that we can help support it, we will.
Thank you.

Thank you. But before I turn it over to my colleague, because we keep talking about FIFA, I just want to ask, because we're a little over a month out, everything is coming, everything is coming, everything is coming. How are our businesses going to know when it's here, right?

Like, is there a huge— at this point it would have to be a huge television blitz to say, hey, now you can look at the information for how you can benefit from
Huh, nobody has a television. No one has-

Something, uh, Council Member Brewer, because I mean, if I go to the website now and I'm a small business and I see nothing, the likelihood that I'm gonna go back 2 weeks from now, a month from now, is very unlikely. Like, we— everyone knows FIFA is here.
Right. So there is something.
As we haven’t done- we haven't done a good job of putting the information out to let small businesses know how to participate in a meaningful way.

Yeah. So as soon as materials were developed and finalized and, uh, an engagement option, like sign up, here's how you sign up. Here's the real call to action. As soon as we received them, they were out in the streets. We've shared them with our staff, we've shared them with the business owners, we've shared them with every single,

uh, business owner that we have on our food and beverage and nightlife night lists. That includes the download and the coordination with the health department. So anybody that's a registered food service establishment from permittee. If they've shared their email address, we've gotten that. And we know that it is the food beverage businesses that are the most relevant here, uh, with this conversation, right? There are other business types, like there's gonna be— I've heard there's gonna be a nail salon challenge where we're gonna have nail salon technicians compete for the most creative, interesting ways, uh, to promote culture and life and countries of origin. But we know that economically, where a lot of foot traffic is gonna come, there's gonna be restaurants, it's gonna be bars, it's gonna be nightlife. And so those are the businesses that we focused on the minute, uh, these, uh, plans are finalized, materials are ready, we're sharing them, and we've been coordinating ahead of time with those agencies so they know they have to— that we want to work on this. We're committed to this work. We're here, um, and that's what we'll be doing for the next—
A recommendation, um, because I know you said of the 56,000 people reached, it's all the food businesses that are, um, registered with the Department of Health.

Sorry, it’s not all— I'm saying, um, all the DOHMH registered food establishment permittees, we— that is, that's included. That's a subset of the 56,000. It's a much broader 56,000. Just a recommendation would be to share that list with New York City Tourism because currently if you go to their website and you look under the different countries of recommendations of restaurants, they may have 4 for each country. So just maybe being proactive because at this point in time it's unrealistic for those, even a quarter of those businesses, to know where to send their information, where to be known. If we already have the data. Let's proactively put it out there to all these people coming to New York to say visit all of these small businesses. So that's what, what we're sharing with those businesses is how can you be featured on tourism. So you could be featured on tourism's calendar.

That's what I'm saying. Don't tell them how to get featured. We should proactively feature all of our small businesses in the city of New York because we have access to their information. I digress. Council Member Hanks.

Thank you Chairs, and thank you so much, um, Commissioner, uh, so in 2022, the Council passed and then Mayor Adams signed Speaker Menin's One-Stop Shop Bill, which requires SBS to, okay, create a one-stop shop NYC business portal which all the applications, permits, licenses, um, related information to open and operate. Uh, the law, Local Law 94, requires that information be presented in citywide designated languages. What information on the portal is available in the citywide designated languages?

Thank you, Council Member Hanks, Majority Whip Hanks. Uh, the portal is available— our understanding is it's available in 11 languages, and it's OTI that handles technology contracts in the city. We advised on the business content for the website. Um, how is SBS working to ensure the

quality of the translations? So we— when— as soon as the website was launched, in our role of providing advice to our partner agencies, we, um, we worked with OTI to further, uh, er, contract with another vendor to to really focus in on the language translation because the— we at SBS felt as though some of the translated material that it was generating naturally was not optimal. And so we worked with, uh, with a partner which included human review of the content across the 11 languages and tried to improve it so it's more user-friendly and understandable to immigrant New Yorkers. And so it was a mix of machine and human translations in all of our pages in the resources by industry section and the business services section, in the emergency preparedness section went through human review alongside, uh, translated vendor experts.

Okay, that's great to hear. Um, now I'm gonna go a little bit locally. So for a business owner, and I heard that you, um, you mentioned Port Richmond, uh, but many, um, business owners in Port Richmond don't even speak English or Spanish. They speak the indigenous language. Um, what about small businesses, uh, and small business

owners who are not proficient in one or more of the languages that is designated by the city? How do we, um, what kind of recourse does SBS provide? Yeah, so I think that's where the city— citywide there's the language line resource where if an agency's external affairs or public-facing teams don't speak a language, there's still, uh, a tool, the language line tool that you could use and our staff are trained on using it so that if there's a communication barrier, they're able to call language line and get translation, interpretation.

And I'll just add, uh, Council Member, that, um, with, with SBS, we also partner with them at MOIA to provide any additional support that they might need if there's an issue that's flagged, particularly with the language of limited diffusion, as you mentioned right now. Um, we step in to support as needed if language online is not accessible.
Thank you so much. May I ask one more question, Chair?
Absolutely.

Thank you. So Staten Island is geographically isolated from the rest of

New York City. Uh, the closest SBS Solution Center to Port Richmond is not on the island. If language access counseling requires a ferry ride and a subway trip, it may not be practically, um, accessible. So is any of this counseling available in person— in person locations in Staten Island? Um, is SBS offices in other boroughs? And because we feel that we have— there's a travel burden. Um, so what is the travel burden for North Shore business owners seeking language counseling?

North Shore business owners can go to our Business Solutions Center in North Shore, right by the ferry station, very close to your district office, uh, and I, I know our teams have worked very closely, and whenever we've had workforce events at the center, we've, we've cross-promoted it. Your office has been incredibly generous in sharing it with your constituents. And- and similar to the Workforce Center, our business center is there too. It's in privately owned leased space, um, but we are committed to ensuring that presence in the north of Staten Island, uh, particularly right by the tip, because we know it's an incredibly public transit-friendly space.

Uh, and if Council Member Morano is here, I wouldn't say that to you since he's not here. I'll say that it's, it's a, it's the best location for the borough-

Yes, it is. I mean, part of the questions that I ask is so my constituents can hear, and then we're— that's just more about education and accessibility, uh, spreading that kind of information. But we are really proud that Staten Island is becoming so beautifully more diverse than it's ever been. So thank you for all your help, and thank you, chairs.
Thank you.
Thank you. I'll now turn it over to Councilman— Council Member Salaam.

Thank you Chairs. Definitely appreciate the testimony that has been, uh, given as well. Just a few questions. As of March 2026, lawful permanent residents are barred from SBA-guaranteed loans. Given that immigrants are more than twice as likely as native-born residents to start businesses and comprise nearly half of New York City's small

business community, what alternative finance mechanisms is SBA deploying to fill this gap, and what is the projected shortfall in capital access for affected business owners.

Thank you, Council Member Salaam. It's, uh, it's significant gap in financing that's been created as a result of the federal SBA's rule change that excludes all but U.S. citizens and U.S. nationals from accessing federally backed loans. Um, and so it's— we can get back to you on a— like, we've done some preliminary analysis and it's in the tens of millions of dollars, it's in the billions of dollars nationally. And it's in the tens of millions of dollars for New York City. Um, and it is concerning, but understanding that we're all in a tough budgetary environment, we are committed to helping small business owners of immigrant descent when they do reach out to us. And if they are permanent residents or others that are not currently eligible for the federal loans, we're trying to scan the universe of lending options available to them through our Funds Finder, which is a website, the first ever capital marketplace for small businesses in New York.

Um, it's called the NYC Funds Finder tool. Uh, and we also— to our business solution centers, we have 7 business solution centers, one in your district on 125th. Um, to the physical center, through the Funds Finder tool, or through the hotline, if somebody calls us, we'll connect them to our financing assistance team. They'll scan what's available. Although there's a gap, there's still some— to some lending options that may make sense for that business, and then help package their application so they can succeed in securing that lending product.

Thank you. And, um, the Trump Administration finalized an agreement allowing ICE to access IRS tax data of undocumented immigrants. If fear of under— I mean, sorry, if fear, if fear of deportation drives undocumented immigrants who paid $3.1 billion in New York State and local taxes in 2022 to stop filing. What is the projected fiscal impact on New York City's tax base, and what steps is the Administration taking to reassure immigrant workers that tax compliance will not be weaponized against them?

I can start. Um, um, what we know and understand is that the impact will be high. I don't have the exact number, but I'll have it before this hearing is over, I think. Um, what has been done is work with DCWP and providing information to small— to, to just individuals. Um, and also, uh, we have been leveraging our MOIA Legal Support Hotline to also provide assessment if people reach out, um, to inquire about whether they want to move forward or not. It's a very sort of personal decision as well for individuals. Um, but I can try to get back to you on the number of what we project the impact to be.
And if I may, just one last— last question.

Um, undocumented workers represent roughly 12% of New York City's hospitality labor force and are critical to healthcare, construction, and agriculture. With enforcement fear driving workers to stay home and reduce courthouse appearances, what sector-specific workforce stabilization strategies are SBS and relevant agencies pursuing to prevent cascading labor shortages in these industries?

Thank you, uh, Council Member Salaam. So our workforce system is primarily federally funded, and what that means is you have to be work authorized in order to get the most deepest levels of workforce services. But any New Yorker can approach our centers for some, uh, some limited level of services, such as just resume help, um, and access to our computer lab. But it's, uh, the deepest levels of workforce interventions, the kind of strategies you're referencing, our system is federally funded, so that creates challenges in that regard.
Thank you, Chairs.
Thank you. I now turn it over to Council Member Brewer.

Thank you very much. A couple questions. When you are— does the city have for the small business— this was during the police, uh, issues— panic buttons? Did that ever pass for small businesses, particularly the bodegas? And if so, how is it used?

So the— my understanding is, Council Member Brewer, you're referencing a city Council proposed legislation. My recollection is it did not

pass the Council, but last year, uh, then former First Deputy Mayor Mastro worked with EDC, uh, to provide panic buttons to, uh, bodegas that are part of the United Bodega— Bodegas of America.
Yep. Um, and, uh, my understanding is over 300 bodegas, uh, received the panic buttons through that program.
Okay. And would that be— would they be trained to use it if necessary for ICE issues, or that's a different topic?

So these are— this is a program that EDC is administering. Uh, my understanding is it triggers, uh, law enforcement response, uh, to the premises. So if you're a business owner, you're a bodega worker, something tragic is happening, uh, somebody is threatening your staff, you press the button and NYPD is then sending, deploying themselves.
But I'm just saying it could also be used for ICE also.
Uh, yeah.
Okay.
Well, I, I would defer to the ADC.
It seems like a tool that if instructed correctly, it could be helpful. I don't know, but I wanted to be in the mix.
Yeah.

Okay. Number 2, um, websites. I don't— a lot of the small businesses do not have a website in the City of New York. I know that from past experience. Are you working— this be both an ICE question, a police question, a business question. Do you know how many don't? Is that something that you're working on? Would it help in communication? To me, when I go now to small businesses, uh, not just because of ICE, all the issues they're dealing with, they want more communication. They don't all have bids. We don't need a bid on every— they don't have chambers.
Hmm.
They need communication.
Mhm.
And so I'm just wondering, um, how many have websites? How many have communicate— what, what are you doing about that topic? Because websites do help communication-wise?

I, I'll start with some of the affirmative outreach that we've done jointly with SBS to the point not everybody has a TV, but some folks do have radio and read the newspaper. So in the past we have partnered with SBS to, um, hold at least 2 roundtables with ethnic media reporters. One that happened the latest, uh, was in September of 2025, and I know we're working on putting some others out in which SBS and MOIA joined, um the core topic was immigrant small business owners and their rights regardless of immigration statuses. We provided resources connected to, um, KYR again, and as well as, uh, information regarding services and, um, initiatives that might be available to them. We also did that in 2024. The goal there was really— it has always been when MOIA leads the ethnic media roundtables is to have ethnic media reporters in the room so they could share, um, information out in multiple languages.
Okay. Anything else for SBS in terms of websites or communication?

So, we provide a 6-module series on digital marketing, it includes email marketing, uh, and other guidance. Um, and then I did wanna

highlight, and I think it's kinda tied to several questions, um, because we know that most folks— there are folks that don't have access to a website or are not comfortable navigating a website. There's a digital divide that is in the city, exists in the city. We have our SPS hotline, and of that hotline, I wanted to share, um, in FY— FY25, we received 9,780 calls. And of those calls, the languages other than English that appeared to be the top languages were Spanish, Mandarin, Russian. Um, and then in this year, FY26, to date, we're already at 8,900— uh, 8,093 calls. So definitely on track to surpass the number from the previous fiscal year. And again, like, it's Arabic, Bangla, Russian.
What are they calling about though, generally? Is it how to get their lease, or is it, you know, something else?

So this is the entry. So if you can't access our website, here's another entryway. Just call us and tell us, I am a business owner, I want to— I have a store, um, I want to open up another store. I— before I sign the lease, do you guys have free legal— I heard you have free legal support. And we'll say, yes, we do. Thank you for

calling us. We can provide up to 40 hours of pro bono legal assistance going through the lease document, reviewing the lease document, negotiating with the landlord's attorney. And so the entryway to our services is the hotline. It's also our website. It's also when you speak to one of us, uh, on staff, uh, in, on the field, in the community. And so we're just trying to make sure there's multiple modes of access so we're not locking any New Yorkers out.
And if one of the services that can be offered is how to get a website, how to do a website. Does SBS offer that service to people?

So we have webinars on best practices of email marketing, website, social media. And whenever those webinars come, if you call us and you say, I want a website, we'll look to see what's the most relevant type of educational course we have available at the time and connect you to that.
Because I think many of them don't have, so I don't know if that's working. Thank you.
Yeah.
Thank you, Council Member, Council Member Hanks. You had a follow-up.

Thank you, Chair. Um, this question surrounds, um, employment documentation and compliance support. Has SBS given any thought to how they're going to address the fact that the IRS has finalized an agreement with ICE to share tax information on undocumented, undocumented, um, immigrants? I think it was like April 2025.

Maybe I can start just to answer Council Member Salaam's question about the data. It's reported that, um, approximately $14.4 billion, um, in the total— so for Social Security and Medicare taxes of $6.5 billion could be lost nationwide according to the American Immigration Council because, um, undocumented immigrants or immigrants as a whole may not be submitting their tax returns via the ITIN. So I just wanted to share that with you.

Thank you. So, um, so if an immigrant worker stops filing their taxes out of fear, has SBS updated its guidance to business owners about I-9 compliance in light of increased ICE worksite enforcement? And where can a business owner

get in-person assistance in filling out employment forms? And is this assistant— assistance available in multiple languages?
